'''''Juniperus oxycedrus''''', vernacularly called '''Cade''', '''cade juniper''', '''prickly juniper''', '''prickly cedar''', or '''sharp cedar''', is a species of [[juniper]], native across the [[Mediterranean]] region, growing on a variety of rocky sites from sea level.<ref name="farjon" /><ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" /> The specific epithet ''oxycedrus'' means "sharp cedar" and this species may have been the original cedar or ''[[cedrus]]'' of the ancient Greeks.<ref>Meiggs, R. 1982. Trees and Timber in the Ancient Mediterranean World.</ref><ref>MARIA PEPLER-HARCOMBE, ALETTA (2011). ''Ancient Furniture in Context: From Ancient Production, Preservation To Modern-Day Reconstruction And Conservation''. South Africa: UNIVERSITY OF SOUTH AFRICA.</ref>

==Description==
''Juniperus oxycedrus'' is very variable in shape, forming a spreading [[shrub]] {{convert|2|–|3|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall to a small erect [[tree]] {{convert|10|-|15|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall. It has needle-like [[leaves]] in whorls of three; the leaves are green, {{convert|5|–|20|mm|in|abbr=off|frac=4}} long and {{convert|1|–|2|mm|abbr=on|frac=32}} broad, with a double white stomatal band (split by a green midrib) on the inner surface. It is usually [[dioecious]], with separate male and female plants. The [[conifer cone|seed cones]] are [[Berry (botany)|berry]]-like, green ripening in 18 months to orange-red with a variable pink waxy coating; they are spherical, {{convert|7|–|12|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} diameter, and have three or six fused scales in 1–2 whorls, three of the scales with a single [[seed]]. The seeds are dispersed when [[bird]]s eat the cones, digesting the fleshy scales and passing the hard seeds in their droppings. The [[pollen]] cones are yellow, {{convert|2|–|3|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} long, and fall soon after shedding their pollen in late winter or early spring.<ref name=farjon>Farjon, A. (2005). ''Monograph of Cupressaceae and Sciadopitys''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. {{ISBN|1-84246-068-4}}</ref><ref name=adams>Adams, R. P. (2004). ''Junipers of the World''. Trafford. {{ISBN|1-4120-4250-X}}</ref><ref>Arboretum de Villardebelle: [http://www.pinetum.org/cones/JUcones.htm photos of cones and shoots]</ref>

===Subspecies===

*'''''Juniperus oxycedrus''''' L. – '''Western prickly juniper'''. Southwest Europe, in eastern Portugal and [[Spain]] east to southern [[France]], northwest [[Italy]], [[Corsica]], and [[Sardinia]], and northwest Africa from Morocco east to [[Tunisia]]. Leaves long ({{convert|10|–|20|mm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=16}}), narrow-based; cones smooth.
*'''''[[Juniperus navicularis]]''''' Gand. (syn. ''J. oxycedrus'' subsp. ''transtagana'') – '''Portuguese prickly juniper'''. Coastal southwest Spain and Portugal. Leaves short ({{convert|5|–|12|mm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=16}}); cones smooth.
*'''''[[Juniperus deltoides]]''''' R.P.Adams – '''Eastern prickly juniper'''. Central Italy east to Iran and Israel. Leaves long ({{convert|10|–|20|mm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=16}}), broad-based; cones with raised scale edges.
*'''''[[Juniperus macrocarpa]]''''' (syn. ''J. oxycedrus'' subsp. ''macrocarpa'') – '''large-fruited juniper'''. Mediterranean coastal sands. Broader leaves ({{convert|2|–|3|mm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=16}} wide), and larger cones ({{convert|12|–|18|mm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=16}} wide).

An additional variety or subspecies ''J. oxycedrus'' var. ''badia'' H.Gay (syn. ''J. oxycedrus'' subsp. ''badia'' (H.Gay) Debeaux) is distinguished on the basis of larger cones ({{convert|10|–|13|mm|abbr=on|disp=or|frac=16}} diameter), tinged purple when mature; it is described from northern Algeria, and also reported from Portugal and Spain.<ref name=farjon/><ref name=adams/>

Other close relatives of ''J. oxycedrus'' include ''[[Juniperus brevifolia]]'' on the [[Azores]], ''[[Juniperus cedrus]]'' on the [[Canary Islands]] and ''[[Juniperus formosana]]'' in eastern [[Asia]].<ref name=farjon/><ref name=adams/>

==Uses==
'''Cade oil''' is the [[essential oil]] obtained through destructive [[distillation]] of the wood of this shrub. It is a dark, aromatic oil with a strong smoky smell which is used in some [[cosmetics]] and (traditional) skin treatment drugs, as well as [[incense]].<ref>1911 British Pharmacopaea: [http://www.henriettesherbal.com/eclectic/bpc1911/juniperus-oxyc_oleu.html Cade Oil]</ref><ref>1918 US Dispensatory: [http://www.henriettesherbal.com/eclectic/usdisp/juniperus-oxyc_oleu.html Cade Oil]</ref> Cade oil has, on rare occasions, caused severe allergic reactions in infants.<ref>{{cite journal| pmc=3207742 | pmid=22675090 | doi=10.1136/bcr.07.2011.4427 | volume=2011 | title=Juniper tar (cade oil) poisoning in new born after a cutaneous application | year=2011 | journal=BMJ Case Rep | author=Achour S, Abourazzak S, Mokhtari A, Soulaymani A, Soulaymani R, Hida M| pages=bcr0720114427 }}</ref>
